title: Mindful life: My annus horribilis
gist: Prospect assistant editor Sarah Collins, in a personal essay, declares 2026 her 'annus horribilis' after a year of illness, bereavement, financial crises and job losses among friends and family. She reflects that seeing patterns in clusters of bad events is a cognitive distortion yet a deeply human tendency.

insights.claim: Collins describes a 2026 in which her support network of friends and relatives was hit one after another by financial crises, health troubles, shock bereavements and job losses, on top of her own lack of fixed housing and full-time employment after returning from Greece.
insights.speaker: Sarah Collins
insights.so_what: Anecdotal signal of household-level financial and employment precarity among UK freelancers and renters.
insights.quote: friends and relatives seemingly struck one after another by financial crises, health troubles, shock bereavements and job losses

insights.claim: Superstitions that bad events come in set frequencies, such as threes, have persisted across religions and cultures since the Ancient Greeks, and the idea of an annus horribilis is strangely comforting.
insights.speaker: Sarah Collins
insights.so_what: Narrative-driven pattern-seeking shapes how people interpret clustered shocks.
insights.quote: The idea of an annus horribilis is a strangely comforting one.
insights.locator: The idea of an annus horribilis

insights.claim: Much of what makes a year feel like an annus horribilis is cognitive distortion from the stress of the first bad event, with human brains — particularly those with OCD — prone to finding meaning in randomness.
insights.speaker: Sarah Collins
insights.so_what: A reminder of recency and clustering biases that also distort risk perception in markets.
insights.locator: Logically, I know that I do

insights.claim: Despite knowing it is illogical, people pin hopes on the turn of the year as a reset, as Collins and a friend do in wishing for 2027.
insights.speaker: Sarah Collins
insights.so_what: Calendar-reset optimism is a persistent behavioural pattern.
insights.quote: “We’ve just got to get to the end of this year,”
